zone: Eastern Pasayten — Horseshoe Basin, the Chewuch and the Middle Fork summits
_areas_note: ONE PEAK WAS REMOVED. TIFFANY MOUNTAIN is not a Pasayten backcountry objective and is not served by any trailhead named for this file. It stands well to the south and east of the wilderness in ordinary national forest, and it is reached by driving from Winthrop up the Twisp River road system to the Freezeout Ridge trailhead at about 6,560 ft — one of the highest trailheads in the state — from which the 8,242 ft summit is under three miles and 1,740 ft of walking. That is a half-day hike from a car, not a trip. Nothing about Iron Gate, Andrews Creek, Robinson Creek or the Middle Fork Pasayten reaches it, and it needs a Freezeout Ridge road entry of its own if it needs anything at all. WHAT IS NOT REPEATED: the Cathedral file already covers Upper Cathedral Lake, Cathedral Pass, Andrews Pass, the Tungsten Mine site and REMMEL LAKE with the Spanish Camp meadows, and the Harts Pass file already covers the Harts Pass campgrounds, the crest camps north of it, Hopkins Lake, the Robinson Creek valley sites, Doris and Freds Lakes, the Shellrock Basin and Eureka Creek meadow camps, Lake of the Woods and Copper Glance. None of those appears below. Remmel Mountain is reachable from Remmel Lake and that is exactly why this file sends it up the Chewuch to FOUR POINT LAKE instead — a different trailhead, a different drainage and a camp nobody else has described. The Shellrock entry below is the high bench southwest of the pass at around 7,500 ft, which is a different piece of ground from the 5,800 to 6,300 ft creek and meadow camps in the other file. THE WHOLE ZONE IS UNDER FIRE CLOSURE AS OF MID-AUGUST 2026 AND THIS IS THE FIRST THING TO CHECK. Two separate fires have shut nearly every road into it. The Ptarmigan Fire closure, running from late July to the end of October 2026, closes the Harts Pass road at the Monument Creek trailhead and with it the Robinson Creek, Harts Pass and Monument Creek trailheads and the Eureka Creek trail, which is every approach in this file to Carru, Lago and Lost Peak. The Sinlahekin Fire, over 150,000 acres by mid-August, closes the Iron Gate, Middle Fork, Windy Peak, Fourteen Mile, Chopaka and Chewuch trailheads along with Long Swamp and several campgrounds, effective to the end of October 2026 — which is the Windy Peak approach. The one thing that has stayed open is the Chewuch trail out of THIRTYMILE, which is the Four Point Lake and Remmel line and was being cleared by volunteers through the summer. Every site below is written as it functions in a normal year; confirm the closure has lifted before planning any of it.

sites.name: Horseshoe Basin — Sunny Pass, Louden Lake and the Smith Lake meadows
sites.capacity: Dispersed rather than designated. There is room for several parties spread widely through the basin, with the usual spots at Louden Lake and around the Smith Lake meadows; horse parties use this country heavily and the good ground near water goes first.
sites.water: The limiting factor and it gets worse through the season. The climb from the trailhead is essentially dry after a tributary about a mile and a half up, and the basin itself is high rolling tundra rather than wet ground — Louden Lake and the small meadow ponds are the dependable supply and everything else is a gamble by August. Fill low and carry it up rather than counting on finding something at the pass.
sites.permit: Pasayten Wilderness, national forest ground, and the permit expectation is the opposite of the Olympic files: a FREE self-issued permit filled out at the trailhead kiosk, no quota, no reservation, nothing to arrange in advance. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is needed to park at Iron Gate. Camp at least a hundred feet back from any lake shoreline. Stock parties need certified weed-free feed and may not tie animals to trees overnight. Campfires are legal in existing rings outside a burn ban, but bans run most of the summer here and firewood in the basin is scarce enough that most parties do without.
sites.notes: This is the camp for WINDY PEAK and the reason the trip is worth doing at all — the basin is one of very few places in the lower states carrying genuine alpine tundra, open rolling meadow at seven thousand feet with bighorn sheep on it. From the Iron Gate trailhead the trail is nearly flat for a mile and then climbs steadily to Sunny Pass at about 7,200 ft at roughly four and a half to five miles, drops slightly to Horseshoe Pass at around 7,000 and opens into the basin; Louden Lake is a little beyond, and the usual round trip to the basin and back is around twelve miles. Windy Peak itself is taken off the basin trails on open ground and is a walk-up rather than a climb, which makes this a rare Pasayten summit a party can reach without route-finding. EXPECT BURN. Every approach into Horseshoe Basin passes through fire-killed forest, standing dead timber comes down in wind, and blowdown volume changes year to year. The last six miles of the Toats Coulee road to Iron Gate are rough enough to want high clearance. Late July through September; the tundra is exposed and there is nothing to shelter behind when weather comes over the border.

sites.name: Four Point Lake — the Chewuch-side base for Remmel Mountain
sites.capacity: Several good sites around the lake with open views to the ridge and the peak, room for two or three parties without stacking up. Lightly used, because almost everyone approaching Remmel comes the other way.
sites.water: The lake, and it is dependable through the season. This is the last certain water on the approach — the ridge above it carries nothing once the snow has gone, so fill here for the summit day rather than hoping.
sites.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the Thirtymile trailhead kiosk, no quota and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Camp back from the shoreline. Weed-free feed for stock and no tying animals to trees overnight; this is heavily used horse country and the volunteers who keep the trail open are mostly equestrians. Fires legal in existing rings outside a ban, and bans are usual by late summer in this drainage.
sites.notes: The base for REMMEL MOUNTAIN, an 8,685 ft pile of granite carrying an old lookout site and one of the great viewpoints of the wilderness. The line in is the Chewuch trail from the Thirtymile trailhead out of Winthrop — a long, gentle valley walk of easy miles past Chewuch Falls with dispersed camping most of the way, to a signed junction at about thirteen miles for the Four Point Lake and Coleman Ridge trail. That trail FORDS THE CHEWUCH RIVER almost immediately and it is the crux of the approach: early in the season with snowmelt running it is genuinely difficult and there is not always a log. Past the ford the grade steepens sharply and about two miles of climbing reaches the lake at 6,850 ft, with a spur into the basin. From camp the summit goes on open ground by way of the Coleman Ridge side, and it is a scramble rather than a climb. Reckon on thirty-five miles and six thousand feet round trip over three or four days. THE LOWER VALLEY IS BURN, repeatedly, from fires in the early 2000s and since, so expect hot open walking, no shade and standing dead timber. This approach is chosen over the Remmel Lake side when the Andrews Creek road is shut, which in recent seasons has been often.

sites.name: The lower Chewuch River camps out of Thirtymile
sites.capacity: Dispersed sites scattered along the first several miles of the valley, including good ground near Chewuch Falls. Most take one or two tents and they are seldom occupied — this is a corridor rather than a destination.
sites.water: Good, and unusually so for this wilderness. The Chewuch runs beside the trail for the whole of the lower valley and every one of these sites has water at it into the autumn. Water only becomes a problem once you leave the river for the climb to Four Point Lake.
sites.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit at the trailhead kiosk, no quota, no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park at Thirtymile. Weed-free feed for stock; animals may not be tied to trees overnight or highlined close to them. Fires in existing rings outside a burn ban, and this is dry east-side country where bans are the norm from midsummer.
sites.notes: These exist to break the walk rather than to serve a summit, and on an approach this long that is worth more than it sounds. The Chewuch trail is gentle enough that a party can cover a lot of it quickly, but thirteen miles to the Four Point junction with a full pack is a poor first day after the drive from the west side, and the river ford above is better met in the morning with fresh legs and lower water. Stopping around the falls at six or seven miles makes the second day short and puts you at Four Point Lake by early afternoon with the summit still available. IT IS ALSO THE PIECE OF THIS ZONE MOST LIKELY TO BE OPEN. When the fires shut Iron Gate, Andrews Creek and the Harts Pass road, this corridor stayed passable and volunteers kept clearing it, which is why it is written up separately rather than folded into the Four Point entry. Expect burned forest for long stretches, little shade, and a trail whose blowdown situation changes with every windstorm. Ask the ranger district before building a schedule on it.

sites.name: The Berk Creek junction and the Middle Fork Pasayten river camps
sites.capacity: A single established site at the junction where the trail up to Freds Lake and Doris Lake leaves the Middle Fork, plus scattered ground along the river flats above and below it. One or two parties each, nothing developed.
sites.water: Reliable — the Middle Fork Pasayten and Berk Creek meet here and both run all season. This is the last easy water before the long climb to the passes, and the country above lives on tarns and snowmelt, so fill completely.
sites.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at Slate Pass or Robinson Creek, no quota and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Weed-free feed for stock and no tying animals to trees overnight. Fires legal in existing rings outside a ban, though the valley is dry and bans are common by August.
sites.notes: This is the hinge of the whole Middle Fork approach and it is where a party bound for MOUNT CARRU, MOUNT LAGO or LOST PEAK actually sleeps on the first night. Two roads reach it: the high start from Slate Pass at nearly 6,900 ft with a short connector down to the Middle Fork trail, or the low start from the Robinson Creek trailhead at about 2,560 ft over Robinson Pass at 6,220 ft, which is nine and a half miles before the valley walking even begins. The high start is shorter by a long way and is what most parties use. From the junction the climb to Freds Pass and the crossing of the upper Eureka Creek country puts you in position for the summits; the whole approach from a road is around fifteen miles. Being on the river rather than up at the lakes costs you height on the second day and buys you shelter, running water and a warmer night — a real trade when the high camps are exposed and dry. The forest here is patchy burn in places and blowdown varies. This is remote country by any standard and there is no mobile service anywhere in the valley.

sites.name: The high bench southwest of Shellrock Pass
sites.capacity: Roughly half an acre of usable bench, so realistically two or three small parties. No established sites, no facilities and no shelter of any kind.
sites.water: Snowmelt and a small tarn below the pass, both of them seasonal. By late summer there may be nothing at all up here and the passes on either side are reliably dry. Carry water up from the Eureka Creek meadows or the river; this is the single most common mistake made on these summits.
sites.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit, no quota and no reservation anywhere in this wilderness. Northwest Forest Pass to park. The bench is thin alpine ground that holds a footprint for years, so pitch on gravel or rock and leave the turf alone. Assume no fires — there is nothing to burn at this elevation and the meadows below are fragile.
sites.notes: This is the staging camp that makes MOUNT CARRU and MOUNT LAGO short days instead of enormous ones, and it is deliberately not the same ground as the Shellrock Basin and Eureka Creek meadow camps lower down. It is a bench at around 7,500 ft immediately southwest of the pass, high enough that every summit in the group is within reach from it. For Carru the line runs west along the east fork of Eureka Creek, leaves the trail at a creek crossing and takes a red talus gully east of the Carru-Lago saddle for a few hundred feet — under two hours from camp to the 8,595 ft summit. Lago at 8,745 ft is the highest thing in this part of the wilderness and goes from the same saddle. WHAT YOU PAY FOR THE POSITION IS WATER AND WEATHER. There is no tree cover, the pass funnels wind, and a party that has not carried enough will be walking back down for it. Snow holds on the north sides of these passes into late July in an ordinary year and much later after a heavy winter, which is the real constraint on when this is worth doing. Larches turn in the last days of September and the nights at this height are properly cold by then.

sites.name: Dot Lake and the Butte Pass basins — the far end of the traverse for Lost Peak
sites.capacity: Informal ground around the lake and in the basins toward the pass, room for a party or two. Nothing developed, nothing signed, and you will almost certainly be alone.
sites.water: Dot Lake is the dependable one and the reason to camp here rather than on the ridge. The basins beyond it toward Butte Pass are dry once the snow goes, and much of the ground between has burned, which makes the shade and the seeps both unreliable. Fill at the lake.
sites.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Slate Pass, Robinson Creek or Monument Creek depending on which end you started. Camp back from the shoreline. Weed-free feed for stock, no tying animals to trees. Fires legal outside a ban but there is little to burn and the ground is fragile.
sites.notes: LOST PEAK at 8,464 ft sits at the eastern end of this group between Monument Creek and the Lost River, and it is the awkward one — it does not fall out of a Carru and Lago camp the way those two fall out of each other. From the Shellrock country the usual line descends to Dot Lake, crosses a burned basin to Butte Pass and then works along a ridge with several false summits before the true top, which is a long day and one that parties routinely finish late. Camping at the lake rather than pushing back over Lago is what makes it sane, and it is the specific advice most trip accounts give: do not retrace the ridge, drop and camp. The alternative approach from the Monument Creek trailhead up the Lost River is a different trip entirely and its camps are covered in the Harts Pass file. Reckon on four days minimum for a party collecting Lost with the others, and note that the burn through here is extensive enough that navigation is easy and shade is nonexistent. Late July through September, and later is better for the passes.
